guardians.name: Bulat

card.essence: the quiet voice: one quiet voice and a guitar holding a whole city's heart (intimacy, wistfulness, simple means). One voice, one instrument, one evening window. Today's drawing: a black cat on a stone sill beside a lit window with a guitar inside.
rhymes: one stringed instrument accompanying a single voice (drop it at Vertinsky, who sang to a piano)
evening lamplight in a window (only where the tradition has its own form for it; otherwise drop)
leave: the black cat and its acting
the plaster wall, ivy, stone sill and window as a composition
the gouache look and its warm yellow
a guitar-in-a-window picture as such

steps.title: Bulat, as he is
steps.medium: Oil paint on a fragment of plastered wall with broken edges: a lit window, a black cat on the sill, a guitar inside

steps.title: after Vertinsky's Pierrot songs
steps.medium: Shellac 78 rpm gramophone disc, 10-inch, paper centre label, in a plain paper sleeve
steps.date: Pierrot songs from 1916; his Columbia (UK) discs c. 1929
steps.link: Okudzhava on Vertinsky, in the 1990 film 'Odyssey of Alexander Vertinsky': it 'pierced' him, an intimate human confession after all the cheerful collective songs. (He is also quoted calling Vertinsky 'the creator of the genre of modern author's song'; I could not trace that line to Okudzhava himself: UNCONFIRMED.)
steps.source: Okudzhava in the film 'Odyssey of Alexander Vertinsky' (Lentelefilm, 1990, part 1, 14:18-15:15), quoted in A. Kulagin, 'Snachala on, a potom my...' (Golos nadezhdy, vyp. 2, Moscow 2005; reprinted in Kulagin's 2024 Vysotsky book, footnote 27): «Меня это пронзило. На фоне всего, что было, всех этих бодрых наших песенок коллективных – и вдруг этот интимный жанр, исповедь такая человеческая. Он был поэтом». (English above is my paraphrase of it.) Discs: Discography of American Historical Recordings lists Vertinsky's Columbia (UK) 10-inch discs of 1928-30, e.g. D31187 (listing seen in search; the page itself was blocked to me).
steps.native: Vertinsky's voice survives as a black shellac disc, 10 inches, 78 rpm, the grooves worn grey, a printed paper label at the centre with the title and singer's name in Latin letters, in a plain paper sleeve. Show the quiet voice as that disc alone, lit softly, no performer and no likeness; if his stage persona appears at all, it is only the Pierrot idea (white face, black costume, a few big buttons), never a face.

steps.title: the Russian seven-string guitar and the romance
steps.medium: Seven-string guitar in wood (spruce top, hardwood body; gut and wound strings), tuned in open G
steps.kind: tradition (his own instrument; he ranks the romance above Vertinsky)
steps.link: Okudzhava bought a seven-string in his youth and tuned it himself; Kulagin reads his remarks as holding the Russian city romance and French chanson 'much more important' to him than Vertinsky. No source I found ties Vertinsky himself to the romance, so this step is Okudzhava's own line, not Vertinsky's (UNCONFIRMED hand-off).
steps.source: Okudzhava, interview (reposted; original venue and date not shown there): «В молодости мне показали три аккорда, показали, как строить — кстати, больше так никто не строит, так что настраиваю я всегда сам, — и я купил семиструнку.» Kulagin (same article as above): «традиции русского городского романса и французского шансона он считает гораздо более важными для себя». Wikipedia, Russian guitar: Okudzhava 'initially used distinctive tunings' and moved to a six-string only in the early 1990s, still in open G.
steps.native: The romance as its own singers had it: a seven-string guitar, a plain wooden instrument with a gently worn varnish, seven strings in open G, photographed as the real object on a plain table, perhaps with one sheet of handwritten or engraved song beside it. Mood is a drawing-room by candlelight, a voice leaning on one instrument; decoration varies by maker, so keep it modest.

steps.title: the torban, Sychra's first instrument
steps.medium: Torban: a lute-bodied wooden instrument with a long neck, a second pegbox for bass strings and a row of short unfretted treble strings along the soundboard
steps.date: Ukraine and Russia, 18th century (the instrument appeared in the second quarter of it)
steps.link: Andrei Sychra, called the patriarch of the Russian seven-string guitar, first played the harp and 'possibly' the torban before turning to the guitar. The hand-off is the player, not the instrument, and 'possibly' is Wikipedia's hedge.
steps.source: Wikipedia, Andrei Sychra: 'He initially played the harp and possibly the torban on which he was reputed to have been a great virtuoso, before dedicating himself to the seven-string guitar.' Wikipedia, Torban: about 40 survive in museums, 14 of them in St Petersburg; it was 'an integral part of the urban oral culture in Ukraine'.
steps.native: A torban of the 1700s: a baroque-lute body carrying a very long neck with a second pegbox at its end, bass strings running free beside the fingerboard, and short treble strings fanned across the soundboard like a psaltery. Show the real instrument, dark with age, strings catching light, in a quiet room, no player; its song-makers were mostly townspeople who sang to it, so the feel is a small private room, not a hall.

guardians.note: The line through Villon does not hold: Okudzhava said 'The Prayer of Francois Villon' has no relation to Villon (he wrote it about himself and gave it Villon's name to get it printed), so I did not use it. Other documented leads, unused: Brassens (his favourite chansonnier, per Encyclopedia.com) and the elders he named (Pasternak, Paustovsky, above all Svetlov). He also named E. T. A. Hoffmann among his favourite writers, a nice tie to the Nutcracker.
guardians.confidence: Step 1 strong: his own words, quoted in Kulagin (the 'creator of the genre' line is second-hand). Step 2 medium: the seven-string is documented, but the romance-over-Vertinsky reading is Kulagin's and nobody ties Vertinsky to the romance. Step 3 weakest: Sychra 'possibly' played the torban, and nothing connects the torban to Okudzhava except through Sychra's guitar. Two of three steps are wooden instruments.

wild.title: A Courtyard Listening
wild.medium: Card, distemper, plywood and tracing paper; imagined theatre maquette in the workshop idiom of c. 1965
wild.link: Codex: Breaks the backward lineage by translating Bulat into scenography: one empty chair and one lit window let a whole city hold the absent voice.

guardians.name: The Glassblower

card.essence: clear glass: one calm, transparent vessel that lets light through and holds a little inside it, native to its time and quiet
rhymes: a pear- or drop-shaped hollow body narrowing to a neck, which is a blown bubble's own shape and is native to every step
light held inside a thin transparent wall
leave: the face: two eyes and a smile
the curled tip as an outline
the scattered flecks of blue, rust, green and ochre
the watercolour rendering and the warm glow as a character
any Apple screen or Liquid Glass chrome

steps.title: The Glassblower, as it is
steps.medium: A single blown-glass drop with a curling tip, flecks of colour in the glass and a warm light inside

steps.title: after Murano's cristallo
steps.medium: Free-blown colourless soda glass (cristallo), hand-worked at the furnace; a goblet or bowl on a hollow stem and applied foot
steps.link: Angelo Barovier's invention of clear glass at Murano: the clarity this guardian prizes is the thing Murano is credited with making for the first time.
steps.source: Museo del Vetro, Murano (Fondazione Musei Civici di Venezia): 'A decisive factor in this turning point was the invention of clear glass by Angelo Barovier (1405-1460) from Murano: for the first time in history glass was transparent, completely pure and like rock crystal.'
steps.native: A Murano cristallo vessel of the late 15th century: very thin, colourless, almost invisible glass blown free-hand into a simple pear or bell shape on a hollow stem and a folded foot, with at most a line of gilding or a few enamel dots at the rim. Its makers' pride is transparency 'like rock crystal', so show it with light passing through and nothing figured on it.

steps.title: after Mamluk Syrian enamelled glass
steps.medium: Blown glass, enamelled and gilded and fixed in the kiln: a mosque lamp
steps.date: Syria and Egypt, 13th-14th century (the Met's lamp: shortly after 1285)
steps.link: Venice's glassmaking grew out of close ties with Syria, whose glass its first makers copied; enamelled glass itself moved to Venice by the late 15th century.
steps.source: Museo del Vetro: 'The art of Venetian glass was a result of very close ties with the Middle East, with Syria in particular, whose sophisticated and elegant glass work was renowned in the Middle Ages.' Met, Enameled and Gilded Glass from Islamic Lands: 'Enameled and gilded glass developed in the twelfth century in the Syrian area...' and 'By the late fifteenth century, the production of most enameled glass had shifted to Europe—to Venice, in particular.'
steps.native: A Mamluk mosque lamp: a thin blown vessel with a bulbous body, a flaring neck and small loops for hanging chains, in pale clear glass banded with gilt and enamel (typically calligraphic friezes and rosettes in red, blue, white and gold), made to hold a flame. Gold and enamels were brushed or penned on and fired once; the light inside the glass is the whole point.

steps.title: after Roman mould-blown glass
steps.medium: Translucent honey-brown glass blown into a four-part mould, with an applied opaque-white handle: the Met's jug signed by Ennion
steps.date: Syro-Palestinian coast (Ennion is tied to Sidon), 1st century CE
steps.link: Islamic glassmakers inherited glassblowing and the use of moulds from the Byzantine and Sasanian empires; Ennion's blown, moulded jug is the Roman-era form of that craft. The Met's sentence says 'Byzantine', not 'Roman', so the final hop is my inference.
steps.source: Met, Glass from Islamic Lands: 'Glassmakers inherited many of the techniques of their forebears in the Byzantine and Sasanian empires, including glassblowing, the use of molds, the manipulation of molten glass with tools, and the decorative application of molten glass.' Met, Roman Glass: the establishment of the Roman industry 'roughly coincided with the invention of glassblowing'. Object: Met 17.194.226, glass jug, Ennion, 1st half of 1st century CE, 'blown in a four-part mold', signed in Greek 'Ennion made [me/it]'; body described as piriform (pear-shaped).
steps.native: Ennion's jug: a pear-shaped body tapering to a flat base, a cylindrical neck, a folded rim and a ribbed handle in opaque white, in translucent deep honey-brown glass, its walls pressed by the mould with crisp ornament and signed in Greek. Show it as the real jug on a plain stand, the colour glowing where light passes through; it rhymes with the droplet by shape alone.

guardians.note: The craft is glass at every step, so media differ by technique and colour (clear, enamelled and gilded, mould-blown brown). The charter's iOS and Liquid Glass talk has no historical tie to the craft; this is a lineage of the glassblower's art, with no person-to-person link anywhere. The mosque lamp's inscription is the image model's calligraphy, not a real verse (real Mamluk lamps carry the Light Verse).
guardians.confidence: Steps 1 and 2 are solid on museum text, though 'copied' is the Murano museum's word. Step 3 is weakest: the Met says Byzantine and Sasanian forebears, so linking to Roman Sidon is my inference, and 'Ennion in Sidon' is the usual attribution, not something I re-checked on the museum page.

wild.title: A Little Room for Light
wild.medium: Lampworked colourless glass miniature in a leather and silk fitted case, imagined nineteenth century
wild.link: Codex: Breaks scale and the solitary-vessel rule: the tiny case makes transparency a precious, intimate feat of craft.

guardians.name: The Snow Queen

card.essence: the hush: cold beauty made exact (stillness, precision, frost glimmer, restraint in colour). One quiet white presence. Today's drawing: a crowned white ermine.
rhymes: a small crown or ring of points
radial or mirror symmetry (the snow crystal's own form); drop where a tradition has no native form for it
leave: the ermine and its black tail tip
folded, scissor-cut white paper (Andersen's own paper-cut manner)
the diamond crown pierced with blue
white-on-cream paper rendering

steps.title: The Snow Queen, as she is
steps.medium: White paper cut from a folded sheet, as Andersen cut his paper-cuts, a snowflake-cut crown, no pins or lace
steps.date: after Andersen's tale (1844) and the 1957 film

steps.title: after Soyuzmultfilm's The Snow Queen
steps.medium: Hand-painted animation cel: ink and paint on celluloid over a painted background
steps.link: The film is Atamanov's adaptation of Andersen's tale; its artists, unable to travel to Copenhagen, drew streets in Riga, Tallinn and Tartu, and made the Queen a cold beauty with no model.
steps.source: Leonid Shvartsman, the film's character designer, in Wikipedia's article: 'In this case, there was no prototype. I imagined a majestic, cold beauty.' The article adds that she was 'modeled as if sculpted by stone' and that Riga, Tallinn and Tartu were drawn on location. (Cel and gouache are standard Soyuzmultfilm practice; the article says only 'celluloid'.)
steps.native: A Soyuzmultfilm cel of 1957: flat, hand-inked and gouache-painted figures against a softly painted backdrop; the Queen as a tall, still, stone-pale figure in a long pale-blue and white gown and a high crown, face composed and cold, in a palace of glassy ice with a few hard geometric crystals. Palette of white, ice-blue and silver with one small warm accent, stillness rather than action. Her movement in the film was traced from filmed footage of an actress, so keep the face generic: no likeness.

steps.title: after Andersen's tale, as first illustrated
steps.medium: Wood engraving printed in black on paper, in a letterpress book
steps.date: Copenhagen, December 1849 (title page 1850); the text first appeared in 1844
steps.kind: tradition (the tale the film grew from)
steps.link: The film's source is Andersen's tale; Vilhelm Pedersen, the first artist to illustrate Andersen, drew its first pictures for the 1849-50 Eventyr. No source says the film's artists used Pedersen (UNCONFIRMED).
steps.source: Andersen, The Snow Queen (Hersholt translation): 'The walls of the palace were driven snow. The windows and doors were the knife-edged wind.' Septentrio facsimile: the tale 'illustrated by Thomas Vilhelm Pedersen, as published in the collection of Eventyr in Copenhagen in December 1849 (official year of publication: 1850)'. Wikipedia, Vilhelm Pedersen: 'His drawings were converted into wood prints.'
steps.native: A Danish Golden Age book of about 1850: black-line wood engraving on cream paper, fine hatching for shadow, no colour, set beside Danish roman text. The tale's own pictures of her are a big sleigh 'painted entirely white' driven by a figure in 'a white, shaggy fur cloak', and a window frozen 'as if they were covered with flowers'; show her only as that, a tall white-wrapped figure or a frosted pane. I did not see Pedersen's actual Snow Queen plate.

steps.title: after Hooke's Micrographia: the practice the tale stages
steps.medium: Copper engraving on a folio plate, printed in black on laid paper
steps.kind: spiritual (the tale stages a practice; no documented tie)
steps.link: In the tale Kay spreads his coat and studies snowflakes through a magnifying glass; Kepler had caught them on his coat (1611) and Hooke on black cloth and engraved them (1665). No source says Andersen read either; his friend and patron Ørsted promoted popular science (UNCONFIRMED as an influence).
steps.source: Andersen (Hersholt): Kay 'brought a large magnifying glass out of doors and spread the tail of his blue coat to let the snowflakes fall on it'; 'They are much more interesting to look at than real flowers, for they are absolutely perfect. There isn't a flaw in them, until they start melting.' Kepler, quoted in the Library of Congress guide: 'specks of down fell here and there on my coat, all with six corners and feathered radii.' The same guide has Hooke observing snow on a 'piece of black Cloth or Hatt', Micrographia (1665), pp. 88-93.
steps.native: A Micrographia plate of snow crystals: a copperplate engraving of many separate flakes, each a hexagon-based star drawn in fine engraved lines and tiny hatching, scattered on warm cream paper with a thin ruled border and plate letters. The Snow Queen exists here only as the exactness of her snow; no figure.

guardians.note: Two of the three steps are prints (wood engraving, copper engraving). The film's Snow Queen was traced from live-action footage of an actress, so no step should need her face. I found no solid pre-Andersen source for the Queen herself; Skadi and Frau Holle come up often but only in blogs, so I left them out.
guardians.confidence: Step 1 solid (Wikipedia, citing Shvartsman). Step 2 solid for the tale and its first illustrations, but nothing says the film's artists used Pedersen, and the plate's exact look is unseen. Step 3 weakest: a parallel practice the tale itself stages, not a documented influence.

wild.title: The Exactness of Flame
wild.medium: Copperplate engraving on laid paper; imagined natural philosophy plate, circa 1665
wild.link: Codex: Replaces Hooke's snow with studied flames: the same precise white reserves hold warmth and motion, testing whether the Queen's beauty needs cold.

guardians.name: The Nutcracker

card.essence: the heart in the machine: a mechanism that moves with care, as if it means well. One gentle figure.
rhymes: a figure made to move by a visible mechanism (key, cams, lever)
a livery that tells its calling: uniform, habit or costume
leave: the green cap and red-banded jacket
the saluting pose
the brass wind-up key as a shape
the Erzgebirge turned-toy outline and its red cheeks
the soldier as the only possible form

steps.title: The Nutcracker, as it is
steps.medium: A turned and painted Erzgebirge wooden toy, a brass wind-up key in its back
steps.date: after Hoffmann (1816), the ballet (1892) and the 1973 film

steps.title: after Hoffmann's Nutcracker and the Mouse King
steps.medium: Hand-coloured copperplate title plate after Hoffmann's own pen drawing, in a letterpress children's book
steps.link: The tale where a wooden toy wakes at midnight and a clockmaker godfather brings clockwork; Hoffmann drew the first edition's title plate himself.
steps.source: Wikipedia, The Nutcracker and the Mouse King: 'The title page included a colored plate of the Mouse King from a drawing by Hoffmann himself.' Drosselmeier is 'a supreme court justice, clockmaker and inventor' who gives the children 'a clockwork castle with mechanical people moving around inside'.
steps.native: A Berlin Biedermeier children's book of 1816: a small copperplate print hand-coloured in thin transparent red, blue, yellow and green, from Hoffmann's quick, slightly caricatured pen drawing; stiff toy-people with large heads in toy uniforms, on cream paper above a letterpress caption. The Nutcracker is a toy among toys on a Christmas-eve table, drawn with affection. The surviving plate shows the Mouse King, so its exact look for a Nutcracker is inferred.

steps.title: after the Jaquet-Droz Musician
steps.medium: Clockwork automaton: brass and steel mechanism inside a costumed figure, a real organ under her fingers
steps.link: In 'Die Automate' (1814), two years before the Nutcracker, Hoffmann's Professor X owns 'the pianist of Pierre and Henri Jaquet-Droz' among historical miniature androids; the Berlin portal notes the automaton motif also appears in the Nutcracker. No source says the Nutcracker's clockwork was modelled on her.
steps.source: E.T.A. Hoffmann Portal, Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, on 'Die Automate': «In dieser Sammlung des Professors für Physik und Chemie finden sich unter anderem Wachsfiguren, Marionetten, Spieluhren sowie historische Miniaturandroiden wie Jacques de Vaucansons Flötenspieler, J. C. Enslens Voltigeur und die Klavierspielerin von Pierre und Henri Jacquet-Droz.» Wikipedia, Jaquet-Droz automata: 'Movements of her chest show her 'breathing', and she follows her fingers with her head and eyes.'
steps.native: The Musician as she stands in Neuchatel: a young woman seated at a small organ in a silk gown, her painted face serene, her eyes following her fingers, her chest rising as if breathing, the clockwork hidden under the dress. Her makers made a machine gentle: show care in the tilt of the head and hands, no gear visible, soft candlelight, and no real person's likeness.

steps.title: after the clockwork Monk
steps.medium: Wood and iron with a key-wound spring mechanism, in a cloth habit; 15 inches high
steps.kind: spiritual (same tradition, older; no documented hand-off)
steps.link: A key-wound figure made to move with devotion, the oldest-type ancestor of the courtly automata Hoffmann's contemporaries collected. I found no source tying the Monk to Hoffmann or to Jaquet-Droz.
steps.source: Elizabeth King, 'Clockwork Prayer: A Sixteenth-Century Mechanical Monk' (Blackbird 1:1, 2002): 'Driven by a key-wound spring, the monk walks in a square, striking his chest with his right arm, raising and lowering a small wooden cross and rosary in his left hand, turning and nodding his head, rolling his eyes, and mouthing silent obsequies. From time to time, he brings the cross to his lips and kisses it.' Smithsonian National Museum of American History; tradition attributes it to Juanelo Turriano.
steps.native: A 16th-century monk automaton: a small friar with a hand-carved wooden face and hands in a plain habit, a rosary and a little wooden cross in his hands, caught mid-step with head bowed and eyes lifted, the iron mechanism hidden under the robe except a winding key. The look is tactile and worn: carved wood, rubbed paint, coarse cloth; the gesture of care is the subject.

guardians.note: The charter's other touchstones are not used: the ballet and the 1973 film are later versions, and the line I chose is the machine with a heart. If a version line is wanted: 1973 film, 1892 ballet (from Dumas's 1844 retelling), Hoffmann 1816. The soldier-shaped Erzgebirge nutcracker postdates Hoffmann (Fuchtner's lathe-turned one, 1870s, per Wikipedia's Nutcracker doll article as seen in search, not re-checked), so it cannot be a step back. Jaquet-Droz: materials per typical description; UNCONFIRMED against the museum record.
guardians.confidence: Step 1 solid. Step 2 solid that Hoffmann names the Jaquet-Droz pianist (1814), but no tie to the Nutcracker's own clockwork; its materials are unchecked. Step 3 weakest: spiritual, a shared tradition with no documented hand-off.

wild.title: The Mechanism of Gentleness
wild.medium: Carved and painted wood, iron clockwork and woven habit; imagined reconstruction of a c. 1560 automaton
wild.link: Codex: Breaks the backward lineage by opening its last figure: cams and linkages make care a crafted movement rather than a hidden miracle.

guardians.name: The Baba Yaga

card.essence: the wink in old magic: wild, clever, a little dangerous, kind to the brave; a dwelling or tool that works by itself. One Baba Yaga, one hut.
rhymes: a dwelling that stands on legs (chicken legs, tree roots)
the mortar and the broom as self-working tools
leave: the red-kerchief roof and the woman's face in the window
the orange cartoon chicken feet with black claws
today's thick outline and saturated red, green and yellow print look
the broom leaning on the door
any pointed hat, wand or owl

steps.title: The Baba Yaga, as she is
steps.medium: A Russian lubok woodblock print, black outlines coloured by hand

steps.title: after Ivan Bilibin
steps.medium: Pen-and-ink outline tinted with watercolour, reproduced in a printed booklet with an ornamental border
steps.kind: tradition (the charter's touchstone); he himself cited the lubok
steps.link: Bilibin drew Baba Yaga for Afanasyev's tales in a style he himself called 'an old Russian style, derived from folk prints and old lubok-fairytales, but merely refined'. (Wikipedia dates the plate 1900 on one page and 1899 on another; his remark describes 1902-04, so it is a little later than the first plates.)
steps.source: Bilibin, quoted in the University of Washington Libraries exhibit 'Fairytales and the Five-Year Plan' (citing Bilibin 1970, p. 59): 'an old Russian style, derived from folk prints and old lubok-fairytales, but merely refined'. Wikipedia, Baba Yaga: plate 'Baba Yaga, in Vasilisa the Beautiful, 1900'.
steps.native: Bilibin's Baba Yaga: a fine, even black pen outline filled with flat watercolour tints, a wide ornamental border of Old Russian pattern, flat planes with no perspective; she flies in her mortar with pestle and broom, and her forest hut stands on its legs behind a skull-topped fence (in his Vasilisa plates). Carved log walls and patterned boards; humour in the sharp-nosed face, never a Halloween witch.

steps.title: the lubok
steps.medium: Woodcut from a linden-wood block, printed in black ink on paper, with a few rough flat washes of colour
steps.link: Bilibin first saw lubki pasted on peasant-hut walls in the North (1902-04) and began collecting them; Baba Yaga appears on lubki, which are her earliest known pictures.
steps.source: Bilibin, same exhibit: 'I first saw Russian folk prints (the so-called lubki) when on location; they were sooty and dirty, pasted up to the walls with bread. It was then that I began collecting them.' Wikipedia, Baba Yaga: 'Baba Yaga appears on a variety of lubki (singular lubok), wood block prints popular in late 17th- and early 18th-century Russia.'
steps.native: A real 18th-century Russian lubok, the famous one where Baba Yaga rides a pig, pestle in hand, to fight the crocodile: a woodcut cut in a linden block, printed in black on coarse paper, with rough flat washes of red, yellow and green brushed on by hand, a few lines of Church Slavonic-style lettering in the block. Her, not the hut.

steps.title: after the Finno-Ugric stump storehouse
steps.medium: Small timber storehouse raised on an upturned tree stump with its roots as legs; weathered pine logs; as shown in an open-air museum (Skansen)
steps.link: Some scholars derive the hut on chicken legs from stilted storehouses on root-stumps used by Finno-Ugric peoples; Bilibin himself studied northern log buildings in 1902-04. A proposal, not a proven descent.
steps.source: Wikipedia, Baba Yaga: 'Some scholars have proposed that the concept of Baba Yaga was influenced by East Slavic contact with Finno-Ugric and Siberian peoples. The "hut on chicken legs deep in the forest" plainly resembles huts raised on one or several stilts using stump with roots for the stilts, in popular use by Finno-Ugric peoples...'
steps.native: A small grey log storehouse standing on a single upturned stump whose roots splay like claws, with a cramped door high up, no window and no stove: the dwelling on legs, with no face and no magic. Photographed as the real object among moss and snow; this tradition made the idea of the hut on legs, not the picture.

guardians.note: Her first firm written mention is 1755 (Lomonosov's grammar), so the lubki are her oldest pictures, and nothing documented goes further back. Propp's reading of her as guardian of the land of the dead is not used. Her plate 0 is already a lubok, so plate II is the real 18th-century lubok of Baba Yaga riding a pig to fight the crocodile: same medium, her own oldest picture.
guardians.confidence: Steps 1 and 2 solid (Bilibin's own words), apart from the plate-date wobble. Step 3 weakest: a scholarly proposal about the hut's origin, not a documented influence, and the lubki do not clearly show the hut.

wild.title: Old Magic, Wound Again
wild.medium: Lithographed, folded and soldered tinplate with brass clockwork; imagined souvenir, circa 1911
wild.link: Codex: Breaks backward descent with an honest later copy: the lubok becomes a walking toy, making the hut's self-working mischief physical.

guardians.name: Niko

card.essence: love in plain paint: one animal, plainly seen and warmly made, glowing against a dark ground (Pirosmani painted a giraffe, deer, sows, calves, sheep). Niko is one animal, never a herd.
rhymes: one animal, frontal or in profile, set large in its field and looking out
leave: the giraffe itself: the long neck and spotted coat
the crescent and stars on its shoulder
the cream-on-black oilcloth look, which is Pirosmani's own manner and must not appear before him

steps.title: Niko, as he is
steps.medium: House paint on black oilcloth, as Pirosmani painted animals: flat, the black cloth left showing as the ground

steps.title: after the itinerant signboard painters of Tiflis
steps.medium: Oil paint on sheet tin: a tavern or shop signboard
steps.link: Pirosmani is said to have learned painting bit by bit from itinerant artists who painted shop and dukhan (tavern) signs, then ran a decorative-painting workshop (signs) with Zaziashvili from the mid-1880s.
steps.source: ru.wikipedia, Пиросмани: «Понемногу учился живописи у странствующих художников, расписывавших вывески лавок и духанов.» (He gradually learned painting from itinerant artists who painted shop and dukhan signboards; translation mine). Also Apchinskaya, Tretyakov Gallery Magazine 1/2009: in the late 19th century he worked in Tiflis taverns 'creating sign-boards, oil paintings, murals and glass paintings'.
steps.native: A Tiflis shop or dukhan signboard of the 1880s: oil paint on a sheet of tin, the thing on offer (a bull, a lamb, a fish) drawn large, flat and frontal in a few strong colours on a bright flat ground of blue, red or ochre, with a painted border and a band for lettering (a blur of Georgian and Russian letters, never legible). Hard-wearing, quickly painted, a little rusted at the edges. Keep it clearly a trade sign on tin, not a black oilcloth picture.

steps.title: after late-medieval Georgian church painting
steps.medium: Earth pigments on lime plaster: a church wall painting
steps.link: The Georgian National Museum's chief curator ties Pirosmani's art to late-medieval Georgian church painting and sculpture; Pirosmani himself said he was no icon painter, so this is a family likeness, not a lesson.
steps.source: Irina Arsenishvili, Pera Museum catalogue 'Pirosmani: A Legend in Naive Art': "The concept of genesis in Pirosmani's art has been put in a broader perspective: the link with the late Medieval Georgian church painting and sculpture, with the so called 'Tiflis school' of portrayal art, and with monuments of memorial character - grave reliefs." Apchinskaya (Tretyakov Gallery Magazine 1/2009): "the entire tenor of the imagery evoked Georgian medieval frescos and icons"; Pirosmani: "I was not an icon painter, I painted St. George only once."
steps.native: A Georgian church wall painting (Svaneti and Kakheti are the usual homes): ochre, red oxide, green earth, lamp-black and a deep blue ground laid flat on lime plaster, figures frontal and solemn with large calm eyes, bodies as simple coloured shapes outlined in dark paint, each scene on a plain band of colour. Its animals (the ox and ass of the Nativity, a lion, a stag) are drawn the same way: frontal or in profile, flat, still, not fussed over. A weathered wall, patches lost to damp.

steps.title: after medieval Georgian stone relief
steps.medium: Carved stone relief (limestone or tuff) on a church wall or stele
steps.kind: spiritual (tradition; scholars name church sculpture and grave reliefs)
steps.link: Arsenishvili also names church sculpture and grave reliefs among his sources; medieval Georgian relief carved the animal, above all the deer, as a sacred beast, and Pirosmani painted deer himself ('Doe against a landscape', 1913).
steps.source: Nino Goderdzishvili, dissertation (2020): "The hunting theme is one of the most important in the diverse iconographic repertoire of medieval Georgian relief sculpture", with 'the cult of the deer as a sacred animal'. Art Newspaper 25 Oct 2018, Arsenishvili: "late medieval Georgian church painting" and gravestones make him a "living bearer of the 'cultural memory' of his country".
steps.native: A medieval Georgian stone relief: one deer (or a hunter's quarry) cut in low relief on a pale limestone slab or church facade, the body a smooth flat mass with a few incised lines for eye, antlers and legs, a plain recess behind it and a rope or plaited-vine border. Weathered, lichen-tinted, no colour. The animal fills the block, patient and frontal or in profile.

guardians.note: No teacher is documented ('he never received any professional education'). The famous champions (Ilia and Kirill Zdanevich and Le-Dantyu, summer 1912; Larionov and Goncharova's Target show, 1913) came after him, so they cannot be jumps back. The English-language 'Persian/Qajar' and 'Byzantine icon' links in Apollo and Povelikhina/Kovtun are 'perhaps' claims; I left them out. The signboard's lettering is the image model's pseudo-Georgian, not real words.
guardians.confidence: Weak throughout: none of the three is a documented hand-off. Signboards are the most solid (the trade he plainly worked in, and Russian Wikipedia's unreferenced 'itinerant painters' sentence is UNCONFIRMED beyond that); church painting and stone relief are scholars' claims about what he drew on (Arsenishvili), and the relief is the weakest.

wild.title: Rabbit in Indigo
wild.medium: Rice-paste stencil-resist indigo dye on cotton (katazome), imagined Japanese panel, c. 1900
wild.link: Codex: Breaks ancestry by moving sideways to Japan; a single warm animal emerges through dye withheld, making tenderness a craft of leaving room.

guardians.name: Emily

card.essence: the one right word: say the most with the least. One small quiet bee carrying one pressed flower, a single careful detail doing the work of ten. Emily is one bee.
rhymes: one small bee, only where a tradition has its own (Watts's busy bee, bees in a vellum margin)
leave: the round striped body, the tiny white collar and the pressed flower held in the forelegs
the outlined flat-colour cartoon look
the sincere-eyed pose and any character acting

steps.title: Emily, as she is
steps.medium: Ink and watercolour on paper, a small illustration

steps.title: after Isaac Watts, as New England stitched him
steps.medium: Silk thread on linen: a New England schoolgirl's sampler carrying a verse of Watts
steps.kind: cited influence (she quotes him in her own hand)
steps.link: Dickinson's poem 'Where bells no more affright the morn' (F114, c. 1859, bound in fascicle 5) quotes Watts's hymn 'There is a land of pure delight'; her family church, First Church Amherst, sang Samuel Worcester's Watts.
steps.source: Dickinson, F114: "Oh could we climb where Moses stood, / And view the Landscape o'er" (Watts: "Could we but climb where Moses stood, / And view the landscape o'er, / Not Jordan's stream, nor death's cold flood / Should fright us from the shore."), noted by Thomas Johnson, in 'White Heat: Emily Dickinson in 1862' (Dartmouth). Poets.org: "There, as a child, the young poet was exposed to Samuel Worcester's edition of Watts's hymns, The Psalms and Spiritual Songs." Sampler: Pilgrim Hall Museum, Elizabeth Gooch (Boston, d. 1747): "It has a verse from a 1715 book called Divine Songs for Children by Rev. Isaac Watts."
steps.native: A New England girl's sampler: fine cross-stitch in silk on undyed linen, a few rows of alphabet, one short verse in stitched capitals (kept tiny and not legible), a border of strawberries or carnations, and a few small naturalistic motifs: a bird, a sheep, a flower spray, perhaps a bee. Threads faded to rose, ochre, sage and indigo, the linen gone cream. A domestic object, small, patient and exact: the verse is the whole point, the flower stitched flat.

steps.title: after Sternhold and Hopkins's metrical psalter
steps.medium: Letterpress on paper: a small metrical psalter with printed tunes
steps.date: London, 1562; this form from the 1584 edition
steps.kind: cited influence (the book Watts set out to improve)
steps.link: Watts as a boy objected to the poor poetry of Sternhold and Hopkins; his 1719 preface says their psalms made the devotion vanish, yet he kept to their few metres, so his hymns could be sung to tunes already known. Dickinson's common metre is that metre.
steps.source: Watts, preface to Psalms of David Imitated (1719), quoted by Robin Leaver, Christian History 31 (1991): "that Spirit of Devotion vanishes and is lost, the Psalm dies upon their Lips"; Watts "chose to restrict himself to the handful of meters of the old English metrical psalms". PDR: "Sternhold and Hopkins wrote almost all of their Psalms in the 'common' or ballad metre."
steps.native: An Elizabethan metrical psalter (John Day, London): a small thick book in black-letter and roman type on soft paper gone brown, each psalm a block of four-line stanzas in common metre, a short tune printed in notes on a staff above it, a woodcut-ornamented capital and a plain ruled border. A psalm is a tune and four lines, nothing more; the bee or the flower, if any, a tiny printer's ornament.

steps.title: after the medieval Psalter
steps.medium: Ink and pigment on vellum: an illuminated psalter leaf
steps.date: England, c. 1320-1340 (as in the Luttrell Psalter)
steps.kind: tradition (the text both versions rework; no documented hand-off)
steps.link: A metrical psalter is the 150 Psalms put into English rhyme; the Latin Psalter was the standard illuminated book they were sung from. Its margins are famous for small, everyday creatures and things.
steps.source: PDR: a metrical psalter is a "versified version of all 150 psalms"; Luttrell Psalter (British Library Add MS 42130), c. 1320-40, 309 vellum leaves, with "marginal pictures of saints and Bible stories, and scenes of rural life" (Wikipedia).
steps.native: A 14th-century English psalter leaf: ruled vellum with a few lines of Latin in black textura, a red-and-blue pen-flourished initial touched with gold, and in the wide margin a thin vine whose branches carry tiny quick-tinted creatures and flowers (a bee, a bird, a flower head) drawn in a few lines of ink and wash. The psalm sits small in a large margin of bare vellum; the small margin creature is as alive as the text.

guardians.note: Her own list of models (letter to Higginson, 25 April 1862: "For Poets - I have Keats - and Mr and Mrs Browning. For Prose - Mr Ruskin - Sir Thomas Browne - and the Revelations"; "my Lexicon - was my only companion") does not name Watts. His debt is real but rests on her F114 quotation, the church's hymn book and scholarship, not on a sentence of hers. Watts's famous 'How doth the little busy bee' (Divine Songs, 1715) is a coincidence of bees; I found nothing tying it to hers. A fully documented alternative line exists through that letter (Keats, then Spenser, then Chaucer: manuscript, woodcut, vellum); not researched in depth here. The sampler's verse is the image model's invention, not Watts's (his bee is "How doth the little busy bee", 1715).
guardians.confidence: Step 1 solid (her own manuscript quotes Watts), though the sampler is a stand-in for how New England met him, not something she cited. Step 2 solid (Watts's own words). Step 3 is a tradition by shared text, not a hand-off, and the weakest.

wild.title: The One-Word Psalter
wild.medium: Electrophoretic pigment display in hand-finished porcelain, imagined c. 2140
wild.link: Codex: Goes forward into a future devotional craft: one bee and “be” compress the whole hymn into existence.

guardians.name: George

card.essence: the meaning in a movement: see the music, hear the dance. One small clear note made visible as a single turn, timed to a pulse, with nothing wasted. George is one tuning fork.
rhymes: a thin looping line (a turn, a track on the floor)
a beat kept (a count, a tune)
leave: the tuning fork and its two prongs
the en pointe pose
the blue-and-gold Ballets Russes gouache look
the small face

steps.title: George, as he is
steps.medium: Gouache on paper, a Ballets Russes costume sketch

steps.title: after Petipa's Imperial Ballet
steps.medium: Pencil on a small sheet of paper: a ballet master's working notes
steps.link: At the Imperial school Balanchine studied under Pavel Gerdt, Petipa's premier danseur, and he called Ballet Imperial a tribute to Petipa as 'the father of the classical ballet'.
steps.source: Balanchine, quoted by the Balanchine Trust: "a contemporary tribute to Petipa, 'the father of the classical ballet,' and to Tschaikovsky, his greatest composer." Wikipedia, Pavel Gerdt: "Among his pupils at the Imperial Ballet School were Michel Fokine, Vaslav Nijinsky, Tamara Karsavina, George Balanchine, and Anna Pavlova." Object: Petipa, notes on the cat's dance in The Sleeping Beauty, pencil on paper, 15.8 x 10.3 cm, Bakhrushin Theatre Museum (КП 107324).
steps.native: A ballet master's pocket working sheet like Petipa's notes for the cat's dance in The Sleeping Beauty: soft pencil on small, folded, smudged paper, hasty ground-plans of the stage with dancers as small dots and crosses in lines, diagonals and one curling path, arrows for their movement, bar counts scribbled beside them, a few words (kept illegible), no colour. The dancers are marks; the pattern on the floor and the count are the dance. (The exact contents of the Bakhrushin sheet are UNCONFIRMED; this follows Petipa's known 'notes and sketches'.)

steps.title: after Christian Johansson's class
steps.medium: Carved and varnished wood: a small violin and a thick stick, a dancing master's tools
steps.link: Gerdt studied under Christian Johansson, the Swedish master who trained under Bournonville and partnered Marie Taglioni; in class Johansson kept the beat with a violin and a thick stick.
steps.source: Marius Petipa Society: "he was always accompanied by his violin and a thick stick that he used to keep the musical beat underneath his mumbled counts of music." Nikolai Legat, taking over his classes (quoted by Jonathan Still): "From him I acquired the very essence of his school ... even to the preference for accompanying my instruction on the violin, rather than the piano." Wikipedia, Pavel Gerdt: "Gerdt studied under Christian Johansson, Alexander Pimenov ... and with Jean-Antoine Petipa".
steps.native: A dancing master's class kit of the 1880s: a small violin of amber-brown varnished maple and spruce with a short bow, worn pale at the shoulder and fingerboard, and beside it a thick plain wooden stick for striking the time, laid on bare worn pine floorboards under cool window light. No ornament. The room is a pulse; the instrument and stick are all the music and all the instruction. (Whether Johansson's violin was a pocket 'kit' type is UNCONFIRMED.)

steps.title: after Beauchamp-Feuillet dance notation
steps.medium: Copper engraving printed in black on laid paper: a page of dance notation
steps.kind: tradition (the French school, la belle danse)
steps.link: Johansson learned in Copenhagen from Bournonville, who learned in Paris from Auguste Vestris, a line (Vestris, his father Gaetan, Dupre) back to the Paris Opera's Royal Academy; Johansson is described as trained in the French style 'la belle danse', the style Feuillet's Choregraphie records.
steps.source: Wikipedia, Christian Johansson: "trained in the French classical style, la belle danse"; Wikipedia, August Bournonville: "directed to Auguste Vestris for training" (Paris, 1824); PDR on Feuillet's Choregraphie (1701): its five positions "largely correspond to classical ballet"; Pierre Beauchamp later claimed the invention as his own.
steps.native: A page of Feuillet's Choregraphie: copper-engraved in black on cream laid paper, the dance drawn as a thin looping track down the page like a ribbon laid on the floor, with tiny step-signs like hooked and flagged notes along it, bar lines crossing the track, and the tune engraved on a staff above; plate-mark and a ruled border visible. A turn is a curl in the line; the music and the movement share one page, nothing wasted.

guardians.note: Balanchine's own 'turning point' was Stravinsky's Apollo (1928) ('the score was a revelation ... I could dare not to use everything', paraphrased; Pacific Northwest Ballet, Mariinsky), a strong cited influence. I left it out because Apollo belongs to the Ballets Russes years, the same world as today's costume-sketch drawing, so it fails the signature test.
guardians.confidence: Step 1: the Balanchine quote and the Gerdt pupil link are solid; the notebook is a stand-in for Petipa's method. Step 2: the Gerdt-Johansson teacher link is solid; the violin-and-stick detail rests on a modern society page, Wikipedia and Legat's memoir. Step 3 is weakest: a tradition by name (la belle danse) and a teacher line, with no quote showing Johansson or Bournonville used Feuillet.

wild.title: The correction, after the turn
wild.medium: Pine rehearsal floor, chalk, leather slippers, manuscript score and wooden mechanical metronome; imagined ensemble, c. 1934
wild.link: Codex: Breaks the single-object framing: the score, pulse and worn turning track make meaning together, with the dancer present only through use.

guardians.name: Rikyū

card.essence: the one flower in the empty room: take things away until what is left matters, and let the empty space be part of the work. One bloom, set alone.
rhymes: a wide margin of empty space around it
leave: the small, uneven black tea bowl, tipped toward you
the morning glory on its rim
black raku glaze as a look
any 'Zen' pastiche: no imitation script, gongs or stereotyped speech (Originality's caution)

steps.title: Rikyū, as he is
steps.medium: A real small, uneven black tea bowl of hand-shaped raku-type earthenware, one fresh morning glory on its rim
steps.date: after Chōjirō's black bowls made for Rikyū, 1580s

steps.title: after Takeno Jōō
steps.medium: Unpainted cypress and green bamboo: a plain well-bucket used as a water jar, with a cut-bamboo lid-rest and a hand-carved bamboo scoop
steps.link: At nineteen, through Dōchin's introduction, Rikyū began to study tea under Jōō; Jōō's tea turned plain household things into tea utensils, and the Omotesenke school says that view passed to Rikyū.
steps.source: Omotesenke Fushin'an: 「白木の釣瓶を水指に見立てたり、竹を削って自ら茶杓をつくったり、あるいは青竹を切って蓋置にするなど、清浄な白木の美を茶の湯に加えることに成功しました。こうした創造的な茶の見方が紹鴎の弟子千利休に伝えられ」 (He turned a plain wooden well-bucket into a water jar, carved bamboo tea scoops himself, cut green bamboo for lid-rests ... this creative way of seeing tea was passed to his disciple Sen no Rikyū; translation mine). Wikipedia: "at nineteen, through Dōchin's introduction, he began to study tea under Takeno Jō'ō".
steps.native: Jōō's wabi tea: no lacquer, gold or Chinese bronze, but things from the house and the garden left plain. A well-bucket of pale unpainted cypress with its bamboo hoops and rope handle set on a tatami as the water jar; a lid-rest cut from a length of green bamboo, still glossy, its node showing; a scoop he carved himself from a slip of bamboo. One thing at a time, bare pale wood, and a great deal of empty mat; if a flower appears, one bloom in a plain bamboo section (a flower holder is not documented for Jōō himself).

steps.title: after Murata Jukō
steps.medium: Glazed stoneware: a Chinese celadon bowl of the kind named for him (Jukō celadon)
steps.date: made in Fujian, Southern Song (12th-13th c.); prized by Jukō (d. 1502)
steps.link: Jōō's first tea teacher was Fujita Sōri, then Sōshu, Jukō's heir; Rikyū is said to have taught 'the craft from Jōō, the Way from Jukō', and bought one of the four recorded Jukō bowls and used it at an early tea gathering.
steps.source: Japanese Wikipedia, 武野紹鴎: 「『山上宗二記』によれば、紹鷗の茶の湯の最初の師は藤田宗理であり、その後、その師であり珠光の「跡目」とされる宗珠の直弟子になった」; 「特に利休は「術は紹鷗、道は珠光より」と説いており」. 村田珠光: 「その四つの《珠光茶碗》のうちの一つを千利休が購入し、若かった頃の茶会で使用している」. Idemitsu Museum bowl: Murata Shuko loved this "clumsy and austere" celadon as "more suitable for tea" than refined celadon.
steps.native: A Jukō celadon bowl, about 15 cm across: Fujian folk-kiln celadon with a thick transparent glaze gone from jade-green to a warm loquat yellow-brown in an oxidising firing, grey-white body showing at the foot, the outside combed with fine 'cat-scratch' lines and the inside carved with a few free cloud shapes. A plain, slightly clumsy bowl, set alone on bare tatami or a plain tray, nothing beside it.

steps.title: after the Song tenmoku bowl
steps.medium: Iron-glazed stoneware (Jian ware) bowl on a black lacquer stand
steps.date: Fujian, Southern Song, 12th-13th c.; prized in Ashikaga Japan
steps.link: Wabi-cha grew as a move away from the fashion for costly imported Chinese wares (karamono); the tenmoku bowl, named for the Tianmu monasteries, was the prestige tea bowl. Rikyū's hand-built black bowls are its deliberate opposite.
steps.source: Wikipedia, Wabi-cha: "tea ceremony had become widespread, with a preference for expensive wares of Chinese origin known as karamono. Wabi-cha evolved as part of a movement to appreciate local wares and simpler styles." Wikipedia, Tenmoku: "Tenmoku takes its name from the Tianmu Mountain temple in China where iron-glazed bowls were used for tea."
steps.native: A Song Jian-ware tenmoku bowl: a deep conical wheel-thrown bowl of dense dark stoneware, thickly glazed brown-black with a glossy running glaze that pools in a dark bead above the foot, pale hare's-fur streaks and a rust-brown rim; set on a black lacquer stand with a flared foot, shown alone and centred, nothing else on the surface. Precise, glossy, sumptuous: the thing wabi tea replied to.

guardians.note: English Wikipedia says Ikkyū gave Jukō a scroll by Yuanwu as proof of enlightenment; Japanese Wikipedia says that comes from the Nampōroku (a text suspected of being a forgery), that only four bowls appear as Jukō's in the earliest inventory, and that the later Jukō possessions (Yuanwu's scroll, Xu Xi's egret painting) may have been added. I dropped those, and anything that would need Japanese script.
guardians.confidence: Step 1 strong (Omotesenke itself, plus Wikipedia). Step 2 good by lineage; 'the craft from Jōō, the Way from Jukō' is attributed to Rikyū and the bowl purchase comes from tea records via Wikipedia. Step 3 is weakest: the tenmoku is what wabi tea answered, but I found no Rikyū sentence naming it.

wild.title: The Place of the Flower
wild.medium: Handwoven rush with linen binding, vessel wear and water stain; imagined study, 2026
wild.link: Codex: Breaks the lineage of vessels by showing the trace of one removed; empty space becomes the flower’s lasting presence.

guardians.name: Maynard

card.essence: the evening the money is for: money and machinery only the means, the point a good life with friends, beauty and talk. One small plump bird at ease.
rhymes: one small plump bird, only where a tradition natively makes one (a manuscript margin, the owl of Athens, the duck weight of Ur)
a measure kept honest (a weight, a coin, a count)
leave: the Omega Workshops manner: bold brushed outlines and flat blocks of colour, the Bloomsbury painters' style
the songbird's outline and pose
any likeness, voice or endorsement of Keynes; no cash box or ledger as his emblem

steps.title: Maynard, as he is
steps.medium: A carved and painted wooden songbird in the Omega Workshops manner, bold painted circles and leaves

steps.title: after the Schoolmen on usury
steps.medium: Ink and pigment on vellum: a scholastic manuscript of Aquinas's Summa theologiae (II-II, question 78, 'on the sin of usury')
steps.link: Keynes read the medieval doctors' fight over interest as an honest intellectual effort, and in 1930 called for a return to the old 'traditional virtue' that avarice is a vice and usury a misdemeanour. He does not name Aquinas; I use the Summa as the standard text they all began from.
steps.source: Keynes, General Theory (1936), ch. 23: "I was brought up to believe that the attitude of the Medieval Church to the rate of interest was inherently absurd ... But I now read these discussions as an honest intellectual effort to keep separate what the classical theory has inextricably confused together, namely, the rate of interest and the marginal efficiency of capital." Keynes, 'Economic Possibilities for our Grandchildren' (1930): "I see us free, therefore, to return to some of the most sure and certain principles of religion and traditional virtue - that avarice is a vice, that the exaction of usury is a misdemeanour, and the love of money is detestable ... We shall once more value ends above means and prefer the good to the useful."
steps.native: A late-13th-century scholastic manuscript such as Bruges Public Library MS 563 (the Secunda secundae): two columns of tiny black Gothic textura on ruled vellum, red rubrics, red-and-blue pen-flourished initials, one decorated initial at the head of the question on usury, wide margins with a few small birds and leaf sprays drawn by the rubricator. Dense, plain and exact; the one decorated letter is the only gesture.

steps.title: after Aristotle's money
steps.medium: Struck silver: an Athenian tetradrachm
steps.link: Aquinas builds his teaching on usury on Aristotle, citing the Politics and the Ethics by name; Aristotle's own line that money 'exists not by nature but by law' is the old form of the state-money idea Keynes adopts in the Treatise. Keynes is not recorded citing it there (UNCONFIRMED).
steps.source: Aquinas, ST II-II q.78 a.1: "Now money, according to the Philosopher (Ethic. v, 5; Polit. i, 3) was invented chiefly for the purpose of exchange". Aristotle, Nic. Ethics V.5 (Ross): "money has become by convention a sort of representative of demand; and this is why it has the name 'money' (nomisma)-because it exists not by nature but by law (nomos) and it is in our power to change it and make it useless." Ethics I.5: "wealth is evidently not the good we are seeking; for it is merely useful and for the sake of something else." Coin type: Agora Excavations N 24585.
steps.native: A silver tetradrachm of classical Athens, about 24 mm and 17 g, a thick, slightly irregular flan struck between two dies: on one face the helmeted head of Athena in profile with olive leaves on her helmet, on the other a plump owl standing and facing us, with an olive spray, a crescent and the letters ΑΘΕ; toned grey, a little worn at the edges. The bird is the whole value of the thing.

steps.title: after the duck weights of Ur
steps.medium: Polished dark stone: a duck-shaped weight with a short cuneiform inscription
steps.date: Ur or Nippur, c. 2100-2000 BC (Third Dynasty of Ur, Shulgi)
steps.kind: tradition (borrowed word and weight system); spiritual as to intent
steps.link: Keynes puts the first state-fixed standard of weight in Babylonia 'towards the end of the third millennium B.C.'; the Greek mina (mna) is a word borrowed from Semitic and the Attic talent is 60 minae, as in Mesopotamia. The Shulgi-era duck weights are the surviving objects of that reform (Keynes does not name them; UNCONFIRMED that he meant it).
steps.source: Keynes, Treatise on Money, vol. 1 (1930), ch. 1: "The first State reform of the standard of weight, of which we have definite record, was the Babylonian reform towards the end of the third millennium B.C." Wikipedia, Mina (unit): "The Greek word mna was borrowed from Semitic." Mainz University on a Shulgi duck weight: stone, 5 ma-na (about 2,500 g), actual weight 2,478 g, inscription tying the standard to the king.
steps.native: An Ur III state weight: a smooth, dark, polished stone (diorite or pyroxenite) carved as a plump duck resting with its neck turned back along its body, the underside flat so it sits true, a short line of cuneiform incised on the back naming the king and the weight in minas. No paint, no ornament, fitted to the hand. A bird that is the standard.

guardians.note: Marshall as teacher is documented (the New Palgrave life lists Keynes among his pupils, and Marshall steered him into economics), but Marshall's own debts in the 1890 preface (Cournot, von Thünen) are books and diagrams, so that line would be one medium three times; I left it out for the medium rule. Moore's Principia Ethica (1903), the book Keynes says dominated his circle, says the charter's idea almost in words: "By far the most valuable things ... are certain states of consciousness, which may be roughly described as the pleasures of human intercourse and the enjoyment of beautiful objects" (s.113); Moore cites Plato's Philebus. A Moore-Plato line is the best alternative if you prefer ideas to money. The 'Babylonian madness' phrase for Keynes's 1920s ancient-currency study reached me only second-hand (NYT review quoted by E-Sylum), so not used.
guardians.confidence: Step 1: Keynes's approval of the Schoolmen is in his own words, but he never names Aquinas. Step 2: Aquinas citing Aristotle is solid; Keynes citing Aristotle is not shown. Step 3 is the weakest: Keynes names Babylon, not Ur or duck weights, and the Babylon-to-Athens hand-off is a borrowed word and a weight system, not a documented transmission.

wild.title: The owl released from money
wild.medium: Hand-raised silver with repoussé and chasing; imagined Athens, c. 430 BC
wild.link: Codex: Breaks the backward lineage by turning the coin into a communal drinking bowl: value serves friendship, and the watchful owl rests.
